However, it is very unusual for political science graduates such as 1 to be able to secure positions which are adapted to their education. We have created a whole generation of people who are not really suited to the labour needs of this country. I am going off the topic somewhat, but when we look at unemployment statistics and at the people who are unemployed or dissatisfied with their lot, we zero in on post-war children who are now adults, people born after 1945. We are the products of parents who went through two world wars and a depression. They worked hard and suffered the deprivations of the depression years. They have said to their children that they should not suffer the same kinds of hardship, that they should stay at school, get as much education as they can and not go in for blue collar work because it is grubby and not socially productive. Almost a class distinction between white collar work and blue collar work has been built up.
So a great many people have completed high school and university. 1 do not know why I went to university, except that my parents encouraged me. That was the thing to do in the sixties. It was only when I was in my second year that I realized what a university education was all about. But many of my contemporaries could not adjust. They could not come to terms with why they were in university. Some resorted to drugs, some to alcohol, and others dropped out. Some went

October 31, 1977
Office of Education
back to the land. We have heard about a back to the land movement.
I go through all this because 1 think our generation is symptomatic of the problem the motion of the hon. member for Vaudreuil seeks to correct. We need a national perspective on education. The hon. member's motion refers principally to linguistic rights-and as I said earlier, I am in absolute agreement with him-but I think there is a second and equally important matter, and that is the impact of education upon the labour market. Only now the provinces are starting to talk about upgrading of apprenticeship training schemes and upgrading vocational schools.
In recent years, in Ontario, we seem to have developed a very successful system of community colleges which teach various trades besides straight academic subjects. More and more students are going into these fields, and they should be encouraged to do so. However, if we had a national office of education, we could encourage people to think of blue collar work as very socially productive and fulfilling.
Last week in this House we heard about the INCO lay-offs, but how many of the people who were laid off really wanted to do the job they were doing? How many were not channelled, in the first place, into a career of their choice? The same question can be asked about people in the public service. There is an old adage: those who can, do; those who can't teach. When the baby boom dropped off, there were fewer teachers, and many graduates who were friends of mine started to come into the public service. I am sure many public servants are unhappy with their jobs because they never wanted to go into the public service in the first place. They never wanted to push paper or make administrative decisions. Perhaps they would be happier welding or doing certain work in a factory.
There is no national system of standards. There is no national education policy which can direct the energies and aspirations of Canadians. I am not suggesting, as the hon. member for Egmont suggested, that the federal government take over education. Goodness knows, we are probably into more areas than we should be already. We should probably be phasing ourselves out of some areas. Education systems should still be run by the provincial governments, but the federal government could establish broad national policies for both the labour market and for second language education.
I have gone on at length and I apologize to hon. members for my rather hodge-podge speech. I had notice of this debate only a little while ago. However, this motion underlines the whole constitutional debate in this country. I see that the hon. member for Egmont agrees with me. I think it was a week ago Friday, when I was speaking during the throne speech debate, that I said within five years we in this chamber would have to come to terms with restructuring, not just the House of Commons or the Senate but our entire system. We need to rearrange our entire constitution.
I welcome this opportunity to put forward some of my views on what I consider to be a fundamental question. The hon. member for Vaudreuil evoked cries of national unity, and it is quite obvious from the way members of the opposition react

every time we talk about national unity that they are scared. They try to castigate our very honourable motives in talking about national unity. Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to speak but when I heard what the hon. member for York East (Mr. Collenette) said earlier today, I felt I had to add a few comments on his speech. He said that the Fathers of Confederation made a mistake when they made the provinces responsible for education. I think he never did refer to 1887 when the Fathers of Confederation lived in Upper and in Lower Canada. I want to mention that during that time the English element represented the large majority and that Upper Canada led the struggle to ensure the right to education in order to avoid being integrated by French Canadians.
This is a little remark I want to make casually, and I think that the Fathers of Confederation have been very wise since these developments; as Canada grew larger we note that the English element was becoming stronger than the French element. Later the French element had a little advantage. The fact that education was exclusively under provincial jurisdiction was a kind of safety valve for the French element. And that is why sections 92 and 93 of the BNA Act have been well thought out for the two great peoples who live in Canada.
The hon. member was wondering whether the provinces had properly discharged their duties in the field of education. If one carefully studies Canadian history, one will find that one of the provinces which showed proper respect for minorities is still Quebec which has properly treated its minorities for the past 110 years and which will continue to do so. If the second language which is made official today by government action has not been respected, it was in the other provinces. If it has not and still is not treated as it should be, it was in the other provinces. So I invite the hon. member for York East to take a look at what is going on in his own riding and to refrain from trying to push the federal government in those sectors which were essentially entrusted to the provinces.
I believe all provinces are anxious to keep the areas they have decided to keep because back in 1887 the provinces themselves decided to keep such and such an area and to leave certain priorities to the federal government. They all decided to leave these sectors to the federal government so that it may rule on behalf of and with the consent of all provinces. I suggest to the hon. member that he reread the beginning of Canadian history, which will enable him to give a sounder
October 31, 1977

interpretation of the BN A Act because today many young people believe that it was the federal government which created the provinces. That is not so. The provinces created the federal government and they unanimously decided to keep those sectors they claimed were under their jurisdiction. That is why today if we want national unity each and everyone of us should have the freedom to act freely within his own province. That, 1 suggest, is the first prerequisite to national unity. He must also be given the necessary means to administer his province. When you wonder whether the provincial governments have been able to fulfill their responsibilities, I think the main problem arose especially from the time when the federal government, sometime in the 40's began to take over direct taxation areas which they had left untouched since 1887.
That is when the provinces were faced with some hardship for the first time, were in need of money, and even today this lack of funds prevents them from providing the necessary services to their citizens in education as well as in all other areas under the provinces' jurisdiction. I feel that as long as we do not give the provinces the financial means to administer those areas which come under their jurisdiction like education, what they need is not the equalization formula but tax points. Let us give them tax points and you will see there will be no more regional disparities because 1 am sure provincial governments are as clever as the central government; they are just as clever and able to administer themselves but let us give them back the rights they enjoyed and the taxation fields they had before the 40's, and I think that as a result we shall no longer say that the provinces are unable to administer such or such an area. Let us give them back their taxation field and then we shall see that the provinces are as progressive as the central government and that they are able to live in Canada while keeping their own identity and being free to act within their own jurisdiction to build a united and free country, through the freedom of the provinces.

This is the worst kind of bargaining! And I cannot accept that premiers, whether they are independent or not, begin to bargain about my rights as a Canadian. As concerns language rights we are all equal, Francophones and Anglophones. I have the right to be at home in the west like in the east and I shall be at home in Ontario. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not a happy occasion for the House of Commons or for the country that it is necessary for us to meet in a special debate tonight to deal with the matters which have given rise to this debate.

On at least four occasions we now know that the security service of the RCMP broke the law of Canada in the name of national security. Incidents that we know about involve the raid on L'Agence de Presse Libre du Quebec, the burning of a barn near Montreal, the theft of dynamite, and an illegal activity resulting in information about the membership lists and the financial affairs of the Parti Quebecois. There may be more.
This evening an Ottawa television station reported that in 1971 security officers infiltrated the so-called Common Front established during that period by the three labour unions in the province of Quebec and, among other things, stole from those organizations documents dealing with their bargaining position and their strategy vis-a-vis the Bourassa government.
I hope that the Solicitor General (Mr. Fox) will deal with this report when he speaks in the debate later tonight. I hope too that he will tell us whether he was correctly quoted as saying that the probability of more incidents coming is quite high and, if that is the case, he will advise us now, tonight, of the nature and the extent of other illegal acts of which he has knowledge.
Those are the illegal acts that we know about, acts in the name of national security. However, it is important for this House and the country to remember that this same phrase has been invoked to prevent the Laycraft inquiry in Alberta from learning more details of a bugging operation, and invoked also to prevent the Laycraft inquiry from investigating the use of an agreement between the Department of National Revenue and the RCMP, an agreement still in effect, which violates the confidentiality of income tax files. It was for related reasons that the government consistently refused to answer questions placed by my colleague, the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen), concerning the activities of various security committees of the Government of Canada.

Attention has focused recently, unfortunately, on the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Naturally, if the RCMP breaks the law, it must bear the consequences. However, many of the activities that have come to light have not been performed by rank and file members of the RCMP, but rather by the special security service.
It is important to dwell a moment on the relationship of the security service to the RCMP. Theoretically, it exists under the Commissioner of the RCMP. In practice, it is directed by a director general who, whatever his relation to the Commissioner, also reports directly to the Solicitor General, and, on occasion, to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). There is a very real question as to whether the activities of the security service are activities which the Commissioner of the RCMP is authorized to control.
That raises the basic question: who sets the policy of the security apparatus in Canada? Who polices that apparatus?
We know who should set the policy and police the activities. In our system, cabinet should set the policy, control the security service, and bear the responsibility for any excesses by the security service.

In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to go over some of the procedures adopted by the government and by the security service in order to ensure that there is indeed greater accountability procedures within the force. This has been a source of constant concern and preoccupation for the government. It dates back to the 1969 royal commission when the government asked a royal commission, made up of a number of eminent Canadians, to examine the problem. It produced a number of recommendations, some of which were accepted by the government and some of which were not. The

government also went even further than some of the recommendations.
In 1971 the government set up the police and security planning group which has received a great deal of criticism in this House. That group was designed to help provide a more sophisticated analysis and to process information coming in. In 1974 we had the Official Secrets Act in which parliament defined for the first time the term "subversion." Within that act, an obligation was put on the RCMP security services to obtain the authorization of the Solicitor General of the day in any matters requiring wiretapping or electronic eavesdropping. While this was only adopted in 1974, previous solicitors general applied the rules of the 1974 legislation within the ministry of the solicitor general before the act was actually adopted by parliament.
In 1975 the government gave a new and clear mandate to the RCMP, which was followed by cabinet directives in 1976, as I mentioned in my speech in the House on Friday.
In 1976 the Marin commission was established and the report will be implemented in the course of the present session. In the spring of 1977 within the security service there was established an operations review committee with the function of examining the operations of the force on a current basis to ensure operations would come within the mandate given to the force by the government, and also to ensure that the operations are carried out within a legal framework. This operations review committee and the director general have access to senior justice officials.
In 1977 we have the new royal commission of inquiry which will be looking at some of the fundamental problems that face the security services. In that regard 1 would very much have appreciated receiving some constructive comments from the opposition this evening about the fundamental dilemma that faces any security service in any country. This is a dilemma that was identified by the royal commission in 1969. Obviously, however, members of the opposition have decided they would prefer to criticize and downgrade our institutions rather than make constructive comments on how we can improve the situation.

I totally agree that it is essential that a security service should carry out its operations within the law.
Mr. Speaker, it is also obvious that under the present provisions of the Criminal Code, some situations are completely nonsensical. For instance, as I said in the House this afternoon, a security officer who would try to secure a code

October 31, 1977

from a foreign country might be accused of burglary. It seems to me that it is a totally preposterous situation which must be corrected at all costs. As for me, 1 intend to make representations in this connection to the McDonald Commission.
Mr. Speaker, I hoped that on such a fundamental matter, the opposition might also consider some responsible ways of amending our legislation so as to prevent such situations in the future.

It seems to me that all of us in this House have a responsibility to ensure that the security services of our country are effective. Everyone here says publicly that the security service is essential to the continued existence and survival of our democratic country but we do not seem ready, in all corners of the House, to give the service the necessary powers or the necessary mandate. Perhaps there are areas in which additional powers ought to be given to the security service as long as additional safeguards are also provided.
It seems to me that if we are talking about a security policy we would do well to progress a little more toward a non-partisan approach because this is a matter which goes beyond the realm of party politics, beyond being a member of the Liberal party, or of the Tory party or of the New Democratic Party, it affects the very survival of this country and one would expect that, when there is a debate on an issue of such fundamental importance, we might be able to count on the opposition making construcive rather than destructive speeches.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while listening to the reply of the Solicitor General to the Leader of the Official Opposition or the leader of the New Democratic Party, it was quite obvious that he felt a little lost and that he tried to deviate from the specific purpose of this debate, because we have not discussed this evening the extent to which the legislation should be amended to avoid a repetition of what has happened. We will have to clear up the matter so that Canadians will know what were the true reasons and the intentions of the authorities when they directly or indirectly authorized illegal acts, acts of vandalism or burglaries.
Mr. Speaker, it is about time that our citizens realize that even in this country there are shameless abuses of power. This is undoubtedly due to the fact that even in our western democracies, we have not yet learned to differentiate between power and authority, so that those who are entrusted with power think that they have the necessary authority and they put those two different things together to do as they like.
Mr. Speaker, I am a little ashamed today of being a Canadian. For years, we have been making fun of some South American countries because the authorities there rule the roost using their police for political purposes. We see that regularly in the news and we think that it is happening a thousand miles from here. Yet, Mr. Speaker, we have had for many years in our own country a dictatorship like those which exist in banana republics and which are using their law enforcing agencies to achieve their own ends.

That is a very serious abuse which we must denounce. People must know whom they are dealing with. People must realize that for the past few years we have witnessed a parody of democracy in this country. Mr. Speaker, when a government has reached the point where it makes use of law enforcing agencies to achieve its own political ends and, which makes things even worse, condones accordingly their illegal activities, the least we can do is wonder where we will end up this way. On the other hand, the government should stop pleading the security of the state over and over again, for the only real agents provocateurs are the very people who are in power now. Mr. Speaker, 1 cannot help comparing this situation with those 1 denounced in 1970, 1971 and 1972. I remember taking part in Montreal in a radio program during which the Minister of Supply and Services spent his time denying what I was saying.
As a member of the Committee on Broadcasting, Films and Assistance to the Arts, 1 was present at a meeting where the authorities of the City of Montreal appeared, and I heard the Montreal mayor, Mr. Lucien Saulnier, the then Director of the City of Montreal, and Mr. Cote, the head of the Legal Services Branch, explain how the FLQ operated, what went on within the various cells, and the Montreal mayor stated that on many occasions he had advised the Prime Minister and the Solicitor General of what was going on. This took place more than a year before the so-called October 1970 crisis.
Mr. Speaker, a police force that sets fire to a barn, breaks into a press agency, steals lists of members of a democratically elected party, a police force that allows itself to do things like that also allowed itself to infiltrate FLQ cells in 1969 and thereby bringing about the crisis we had in 1970. 1 know this is a very serious charge I am making, Mr. Speaker, but I maintain it because it is time that once and for all the Canadian population know that there are in this country people who have lost their reason, people who cannot accept the changes that are taking place in Quebec, people who only a few months or at most a year ago thought Quebec emancipation and free development were only velleities, people who spend days and nights trying to find a way of crushing people who only want to be free and happy.
When people have such an erroneous idea of the collective "vouloir etre" of a whole nation, of a whole people, they try by all means to justify a radical and unreasonable action against these people and, as these people do not take such actions, they are the first ones to provoke them to justify before the whole country their efforts to crush down this emancipating movement which is originally a very sound one.
They will say yes to destroy the country. Let us stop those idiocies. How many Quebecers are there now in power in Quebec as here in this House? Since when did they suggest they wanted to destroy the country when all they want is to reorganize it, to restructure it so its fundamental entities could really be free and equal? Why call all those who want to free themselves and their minds, why call them terrorists, why

October 31, 1977

accuse them of threatening state security? No, Mr. Speaker, that game has just been unveiled.
Mr. Speaker, those who have been using negativism for years to try and destroy the basic aspirations of a whole nation are getting back smack in the face today the result of that boomerang they dared throw. It is not surprising that today if we know certain very specific facts and very specific circumstances it is because the government objectively decided to reveal those facts and circumstances. Absolutely not, Mr. Speaker! The only reason that forced the Solicitor General (Mr. Fox) to make the statements he made Friday was that he knew quite well that in any case following the line of action taken by the government of Quebec the Keable Commission was there, and those things were going to come out. They decided in favour of a policy of lesser evil and to disclose themselves what they knew was going to come out in a couple of weeks or months. And even the minister says there could be more. Mr. Speaker, it is too bad, we have gone beyond that stage where we could be made to believe stories by individuals more concerned with partisan struggles than anything else. 1 talked today of the stupefaction that gripped a lot of Canadians when 1 pointed out that that revelation had astounded several people. Well, today I received by special delivery a letter from a citizen who is not happy with what is going on. This will become generalized and those who will have provoked Canadian citizens will have to suffer the consequences. I would like to quote from this letter dated October 28, 1977. I shall not mention the name of the man concerned to avoid the possibility that the RCMP will break into his premises, but this Friday, since this letter is dated October 28, 1977, from Ville LaSalle, when this man heard on television what was happening, he sat down at his desk and took his pen to write me a letter. Why? Because he was greatly indignant. Here are a few passages from this letter:
Sir, I maintain that it is inconceivable for such a thing to have happened. Is all this not a follow-up on the October 1970 crisis, for which, in passing, the war measures are still in force? Is this action aimed at suppressing the right of anyone to belong to the political party of his choice? There is every reason to believe that certain people want and look for provocation. There are indications that certain people try to hide the truth. If certain present and past members of Parliament and ministers of this government have acted and are still acting hypocritically, the public is entitled to know.
As a citizen of Quebec and a Canadian-
-and he says in brackets-
-(for the moment) and as a member of the Parti Quebecois and a federal government employee, I demand that the actions of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police come to light and that the present government, the Prime Minister, the ministers and the Solicitor General be asked to reply to certain questions. I have known for a long time, sir, that we are being watched, but I refuse to be used as a political tool and for the political purposes of the Liberal party.	.
As a French-speaking member of parliament from Quebec, you must urgently ask these questions in the House. If certain people wanted to bring together the present Quebec government and the federal government, theirs is definitely a lost cause in view of these developments. If we must now come back to a "Believe or die" attitude, I would prefer to die. It is only through a public inquiry and with impartial people (not Liberals)-
(Mr. Matte.]
-this is between brackets-
-that we will be able to get to the truth as far back as October 1970.
What has just come to light, Sir, is the straw that broke the camel's back. Small wonder then that we should have witnessed so much commotion on the part of this government since November 15, 1976 in an effort to do as much harm to the present Quebec government through all sorts of statements and commissions.
Mr. Speaker, I read the spontaneous reaction of a Canadian citizen who is a member of the Parti Quebecois, which he chose freely and who, 1 hope, enjoys that freedom; and now this fellow learns that this list was in the hands of my friends across the way. If one stops to think of it even briefly, it is absolutely awful. The former speakers asked a lot of questions, which of course were not answered: but how did that ever happen? How come we learn in 1977 what was known to be illegal and irregular in 1975, as the right hon. Prime Minister said himself, and even in 1975? How did that happen? Does that mean that, had it not been for special circumstances, no one would have known those actions were taken? No, we cannot accept such things. How many other similar activities may have taken place, and what, if we go back further than 1973? As far as I know, in 1973 nothing special could justify such actions; so, if that is the case, if we let those who are in power also have the authority to decide whether or not they can do this or that, then democracy is done for.
Mr. Speaker, the worst has happened to democracy, it is done for. Anyone can be a suspect, the hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Matte), the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette), or any member of this House. Under the pretext of the security of the state, electronic devices are put in offices, homes are being searched and documents are taken from files. It is frightening, Mr. Speaker, and 1 do not believe the leaders of a country should be allowed to behave in this way because of an unfortunate incident that happened in 1970. And as I said earlier, I believe it has been brought on by these same individuals. When a situation of this kind arises, serious questions are being asked and we must have answers. It is said, and the minister repeated it, the McDonald inquiry now in progress will reveal a number of things.
Mr. Speaker, once more I agree with the previous speakers who say that the terms of reference of this inquiry do not confer all the authority, all the power to bring out the whole truth. Such an inquiry should go back to the years 1970, 1969, 1963. Such an inquiry must go back to the time of the Maison du Pecheur in Perce, when RCMP officers were members of FLQ cells. That inquiry must go back to every incident that happened through the years, the blame for which was put on Quebecers in order to tarnish their ideology.
Mr. Speaker, those times are over. We must have the truth so the people can judge the actions of their leaders. Mr. Speaker, there have been too many serious incidents, the ramifications of which could have been more disastrous still than has been experienced. There have been too many tragic incidents indeed for their causes and reasons to remain untold.
I therefore ask that the light be made not only on the break-in that secured a list of members of a political party, but also that an inquiry be made into what extent the RCMP infiltrated the FLQ and are therefore responsible for certain acts that have
October 31, 1977

been perpetrated during that difficult period we went through. It should need to be explained, for instance, how come RCMP officers were tenants in the apartment above that in which James Cross was held prisoner.
Mr. Speaker, all those questions will have to be answered. All these circumstances must be brought into light under which the government lost their heads. Because this is the kind of nonsense that happens when one loses one's head. And when on November 15 we heard the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and other ministers come one after the other to utter the most horrendous stupidities, they proved once more they were losing their heads. It is a dangerous thing to be governed by people who lose their heads. This is why the people must be informed. Hypocrisy must be exposed. We must know exactly who we are dealing with, what kind of people we have as a government, because in my view they are getting less and less worthy of it.
So, and I would conclude on this, let not the Solicitor General think that we do not want to be constructive. We do want to be constructive to the extent we want the government to get out of there. After abusing their powers, after tampering directly with individual freedoms, they have no right to be there any more. This is being constructive. When the people find that some government went contrary to the bill of rights itself it is in my view a very constructive step to get rid of individuals that are now trampling on liberty and democracy in this country.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to the remarks of my hon. friend, the Solicitor General (Mr. Fox). 1 agree with the previous speaker, the hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Matte), that the Solicitor General did not really come to grips with the substance of what we are discussing here tonight.
1 must say at the outset, Mr. Speaker, that the Solicitor General is wrong when he suggests that we are trying to try the RCMP in the House of Commons. What we are seeking to do is to get information about this incompetent government. The Solicitor General has said, in effect, that we have not dealt so far with matters of substance. Well, he is a fine one to say that under the circumstances, but I want to assure him that I and members of my party do in fact have matters of substance and policy which we have worked on, and which we are prepared to put forward at any time. But 1 think it is asking a bit much tonight, under the circumstances, for me personally to make the type of speech I intended to make, in which 1 intended to bring up, among other things, some of the background of the RCMP, as this force has evolved from a territorial force into our national police force, with constitutional complications in the process.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, there are, as it is becoming more and more evident, complications between Section 92(14) of the BNA Act, which gives exclusive jurisdiction over the administration of justice to the provinces, and some other sections,

such as perhaps Section 91(7), which do not, in my opinion, necessarily give the RCMP the kind of mandate which it has had to assume because of the neglect of this government in implementing some of the recommendations of the Mackenzie commission, which were made ten years ago.
1 intended to deal, Mr. Speaker, with a lot of other matters of substance; to put forward my thoughts on why the Minister of Justice and Solicitor General of Quebec Marc-Andre Bedard, has found it necessary apparently to threaten to put the RCMP under the Quebec police commission; as to why the Solicitor General of Alberta, Mr. Foster, has had to complain publicly at the highest levels of the RCMP about the kind of intrusion into provincial jurisdiction which the force and federal authorities have found it necessary for their purposes to perpetrate. I had intended to do a lot of these things, Mr. Speaker, but under the circumstances, in view of some of the relations which have come forward, I want to say a few things tonight about my own experiences in the House, and about the lack of frankness and the lack of facts which I have encountered.
1 want to say to the Solicitor General that when he deals with facts I will stake my record in this House against his.

Mr. Speaker, this evening, despite the importance of the debate, one realizes with regret that discussions are inspired more by political considerations than the will to find a sound solution to the problem. When one hears hon. members of the opposition speak of the PQ, when one realizes to what extent they are outraged by the possibility that the offices of a legal political party may have been broken into illegally, well, first of all as a Quebecer 1 really feel embarrassed to see that the police force of the federal government, as well as some provincial police forces such as the Quebec Police, or that the police of the city of Montreal should be implicated in certain events which, to say

the least, leave us perplexed. But when people talk of the climate in 1973, and members of the opposition speak of the climate in 1975, a few years are being overlooked, Mr. Speaker.
In Quebec and Canada but more particularly Quebec since this matter deals with a Quebec political party, we tend to forget that back in 1964 a few bombs exploded here and there and that acts of terrorism, alien to our way of life, took place in subsequent years. One can argue about violations of individual and collective liberties but it must be admitted that most unusual events happened including the murder of a provincial minister. These are things, Mr. Speaker, that we should remember. A peculiar phenomenon took place. This may be the kind of phenomenon that happens in a country in the midst of an evolution, Mr. Speaker, but a few months ago Premier Rene Levesque himself, in a radio broadcast, on the CBC network stated that during a newsmen labour conflict he felt rather uncomfortable because some of the strikers who wanted to be associated, on this occasion at least, with members of the Parti Quebecois in a protest march had asked him to join them in the street. But, in his capacity of leader of a responsible party he felt he could not have anything to do with fanatics. And he explained on the CBC how sorry he was to have to turn down the offer of people sympathetic to his cause but he felt that in this crowd several thousands strong there were a few fanatics that the PQ could not afford to identify itself with.
Mr. Speaker, I think that we should refine our thinking when entering this debate. I think that too much of an attempt has been made to single out the RCMP for what has been referred to as illegal break-ins. Our various police forces in Canada, at the three levels of government, had to face new situations. 1 do not think I am in any way blaming or criticizing them when I say that these police forces, within the North American context, may not have been trained to deal with an unexpected state of affairs. That is why those people had to adopt new strategies and new procedures. I think this debate tonight would be most positive if all hon. members would recognize that our police forces may have been excessive in some operations and should redefine their operation procedures, but if it is true that the office of the Parti Quebecois was broken into the way some opposition members suggested, I think that the Solicitor General of Canada (Mr. Fox) was very clear on that point.
He is asking the Quebec attorney general to bring the facts to light and let him investigate and if the judiciary system of the province of Quebec concludes that there was indeed illegal action, I think that we should not be partisan and should help the police force for which we are responsible-the RCMP-to adopt a new rule to ensure individual and collective liberties.
Mr. Speaker, I will always be opposed at any time in this country to a police force restricting opinions, ideas and spoken words and restricting also the right of individual action if such actions are legal and non-violent. As my friend from New
October 31, 1977

Westminster (Mr. Leggatt) mentioned it earlier, it is possible, even desirable, that all Canadians be free to criticize, disagree completely with the government but, Mr. Speaker, 1 believe there is a way to do it, a non-violent way, by democratic ways, and we have the responsibility to protect them.
Mr. Speaker, it is not only because of opposition pressures that the government instituted the McDonald Commission. When this commission was established, it was given a very comprehensive mandate and we would very much like to hear the opposition parties, for instance, my colleague from Joliette (Mr. La Salle), make recommendations to this commission so as to develop precise rules which will meet the new aspirations of Canadian citizens and which will ensure the basic freedoms that Canadians have always enjoyed and must be preserved for always.
1 believe that such proposals should be made and that we should now be able to ask ourselves some questions. This should be the purpose of this evening's sitting, to ask ourselves some questions to know how our security services can, first of all truly ensure the security of the state and its citizens, and secondly, not become a politically controlled institution. It is difficult to strike a happy medium. Our colleagues opposite ask that the government see to it that the police does not exceed certain limits, but in some other debate or at another time, the same people tell us that the government controls the police and uses it for political purposes. They should tell us clearly and once and for all if they want us to leave the police to its own devices or if they want us to give instructions to the police and to the security council.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that the debate concerns one of the most basic issues of the history of this country and I wish the members of the House would quickly pass over their pet subject and make truly positive recommendations. If they are not ready to make them tonight, 1 hope they will at least make them eventually and as soon as possible to the proper institution which is the McDonald Commission. It is a matter of proposing standards, procedures that will allow our security service to be efficient and serve Canadians without infringing on the rights and freedom of its citizens.

We ask questions here and we ask questions in the committee, but we come away with about as much information as we got today, namely, zilch-nothing. The obsession with secrecy shown by the government does nothing to enhance our confidence in it.
There were reasons for the setting up of the security, planning and research group, as it was then known-the sham of "research" soon disappeared. But the reasons were not those given by the present Solicitor General (Mr. Fox). They go back to 1963 when the Spence inquiry was under way, when the Munsinger inquiry was under way, and when other questions of national security were being discussed in the House. That report was the reason for the creation of the Royal Commission on Security, a report which, incidentally, the Prime Minister promised would be debated in the House. But he reneged on that promise as he did on so many others.
That group of civilians was set up for four purposes. They were these: first, to infiltrate and instal agents for the purpose of gaining intelligence from the educational system. Without going into great detail I call the attention of the House to the surveillance conducted on university campuses.
Second was the infiltration and surveillance of the public service itself-the "extra-parliamentary opposition" with which operation the former solicitor general is familiar since the famous blacklist was prepared under the leadership of the Minister of Supply and Services.
The third reason was that of infiltrating and obtaining intelligence from the mass media, and the fourth was for the same purpose with respect to the labour movement. Those were the four objectives in setting up what is referred to as this non-operational group of civilians originally known as SPARG and subsequently as SPAG and SPA. The group had regional desks in all these areas with civilian representatives as well as RCMP.
It all stemmed from the preparation of a paper on "The Management of Crisis" by General Dare, who was subsequently smuggled into the RCMP, probably being the first non-member of the force to be appointed to the post of officer in the RCMP, with one exception, that of General Bourne. It is traditional in the force that the post of commissioner is filled from within its ranks. That tradition has been followed throughout the entire existence of the RCMP. Today there is some fear that the commissioner might be drawn from outside the force, a very sad development should it occur.

When the debate arose in this House on the setting up of that special agency in 1969 we resisted its formation on the basis that there was a real danger of it being subverted into being a political state police force. We predicted in that debate in 1969 that if such an agency were set up precisely what has happened now would happen. And it has come to pass. What has taken place is this: the RCMP, having previously enjoyed a standard of integrity unmatched in the world, has now been eroded to a point at which the public of Canada is justified in presuming-and I state this as my conviction-that there is an unwarranted interference with the operations of a previously independent police force in the performance of its functions. This has been done while assuring the country that there is a real need for this civilian agency in order to protect national security. That is only a guise.
The quickest way of restoring the confidence of the public in the integrity of the force is to abolish that agency and place the responsibility for security and intelligence back under the sole control of the force where it has rested for a hundred years.
With regard to the four objectives of this agency let me inform hon. members that there were 14 groups which the agency was charged with infiltrating and gathering intelligence from. The Globe and Mail apparently has made public the name of one of these groups. I want to put the whole 14 on the record. One was the FLQ, a natural group to warrant the investigation of any security-minded country. Another was the National Farmers' Union.

The Saskatchewan Metis Association was one of the objectives of the group, and the memorandum to which 1 have referred was directed to that very group. It is dated August 25, 1972, and directed to W. J. Dabros, if the Solicitor General wants to check the memorandum and verify the facts I am putting on record.
The next is a most interesting group which the civilian agency was charged with infiltrating for the purpose of gathering intelligence, in 1969 I remind hon. members having regard for the events that transpired earlier this year. It was to get into the extra parliamentary opposition and alter the structure of the existing government. There are some very interesting names which 1 will not put on the record with regard to the activity of this civilian agency.

One of the names which came up as a result of conversation 1 had in order to glean this information was the name of Bernard Ostry, who, I am sure, is familiar to a good many members on the other side. There is a very interesting name here in connection with the next organization that was to come under the surveillance of this agency. The New Left, a philosophical movement. Another one was The New Morning, a maritime group oriented toward guerilla warfare. On October 16, 1971, this group demonstrated against Canadian Forces Headquarters in the maritimes. Molotov cocktails were thrown.
Another group was the Black United Front, headquartered in Halifax. The Local Initiatives Program and National Health and Welfare came under the scrutiny of the early SPARG. The agency was charged with consulting Liberal cabinet aides with regard to any LIP grant that came under investigation to see whether the investigation should continue or be dropped.
The next group that came under the scrutiny of this civilian police agency was the Acadians, again based in the maritimes, Moncton. The next was The Red Morning, another new left organization based in Toronto. They commenced in 1970 with rifle and guerilla training and had links with the Black Panthers and Weathermen.
I might interject that another of the responsibilities of the group was to recruit agents wherever they could get them for the purpose not only of infiltrating these groups whose names I am putting on the record, but also for the purpose of infiltrating university campuses, the media, labour, and national political organizations as well as government. I might interject as well that on unimpeachable authority it came to me that this agency had two sources of information in the office of the then Leader of the Opposition, the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield), who just stepped down from leadership of this party.
Next was the Communist Party of Canada, the Marxist-Leninist movement, very heavy in Vancouver. The smoke bombing of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation headquarters in Toronto was one of the matters which gave rise to the attention of this agency and this group.
Not unsurprisingly, Praxis was the name of another group which occupied the focused attention of SPARG, now SPAG. Not surprising too was the Edmund Burke Society.
Those people who come from the province of Quebec will be interested to learn that the agency was specifically charged to speak about guidelines and speak about a cabinet committee on security and the control which the politicians exercised over this group. There was a list of subversive organizations. These were three that were listed as subversive to occupy the atten-

tion of this agency in the province of Quebec: the Quebec Teachers' Corporation, the CNTU, and the Quebec Federation of Labour.

It will surprise hon. members, but possibly not some of those opposite and certainly not the Solicitor General and his predecessors, that all of this activity was funded without benefit of approval of any estimates by parliament. That is where the money was gleaned from so that we parliamentarians would not be able to put our fingers on the operations of this agency.

In other words, if the rule of law was infringed-and it probably was, it appears that it was-then it was infringed by the police, not by the government. If there is government responsibility, it cannot be found under the principle of the rule of law; it must be found under the principle of ministerial responsibility.
1 should like to turn now to a consideration of that other principle, the great democratic principle, as the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby called it. Here the meaning is that responsibility must be commensurate with authority. To the extent that the executive has authority, it must be responsible for how the authority is executed. If a politician enjoys the benefits, then he must accept the blame which results from the exercise of the powers directly under his control.
Obviously, Mr. Speaker, when we speak of government and of ministerial responsibility we are dealing with what philosophers would call an analogous concept. We are dealing with something which is different in a lot of respects and in a lot of instances, because not all the instances are the same. I will not go into an analysis of all the organs of government tonight, but I would certainly argue that when we are dealing with an independent agency, such as the police or the RCMP, the application of the principle of ministerial responsibility has to be almost wholly different from the application of that principle to an ordinary department of government.
The principle can be applied to the police only in a very limited sense in order to avoid political interference. The accountability of the ministry in a case of this kind is only to ensure that, when there is fault, change takes place in the agency. My argument is based on the principles of the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby himself, who put the rule of law

in the first place, gave it priority of place with respect to democratic principles, putting in second place the principle of ministerial responsibility. If there is a conflict, the principle of the rule of law governs.
In this case, since the rule of law insists that there be absolute impartiality in the administration of justice free from external direction, especially political direction, this could not be achieved if the minister were to assume total responsibility for all the actions of the agency.
We have a government which has assumed its responsibility. It has stopped the surveillance of the PQ which was taking place, as soon as it found out about the-

In addition to stopping the surveillance of the PQ, the government consulted regularly with top officers in the RCMP in an attempt to find out the facts. In many cases it seemed that the top officers themselves did not know the facts. There seems to have been a persistent policy in the force in recent years to deny even the top officers in the force knowledge of what was being done lower down, and sometimes not that much lower down either.
The government also gave a full account to the government of Quebec, which was the concerned government in charge of the administration of justice in the area where the offences took place, so that it could lay charges according to the normal juridical process. Finally it set up a royal commission with very broad terms. In addition to those terms, the government promised with complete co-operation.
My interpretation of that is that the government will change the terms of reference of that royal commission, if the royal commission should request additional powers to enable them to fulfil their mandate, and that the ministers will co-operate completely with the royal commission in appearing before it as witnesses if they are summoned. Mr. Speaker, let me say at the outset that I hope to be able to reach a common ground with all members of the House of Commons. 1 think we all believe that there is one law for all Canadians and that the rule of law must not be different for those in authority and those in ordinary walks of life, and that when the rule of law is broken, no matter by whom and in what position, they should bear the full brunt of the law.
If the law is broken, prosecution should follow the ordinary course. If the evidence is there, it should be brought before a judge and jury. No matter who has broken the law, they must face the consequences of their act.
It should not take more than the first year in Sunday school or the first year in catechism class, let alone the first year in law school, to know that it is wrong to break and enter or to steal.
These are fundamental things, but I become sickened when I hear hon. members opposite, in pious righteousness, continue to condemn the RCMP. They condemn them time after time, speaker after speaker, saying that they have not been doing the right things in this country.
Usually the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leg-gatt) is one of the most sane and sensible members of this House, but tonight he said it is the opposition which is protecting the RCMP. The truth is anything but that. Every hon. member opposite who has spoken has condemned the RCMP and its operations, if not directly then indeed by the innuendo drifting from their mouths in every statement they make. It is shameful.
We on this side of the House have said that the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) continually makes innuendoes without having the guts to make any direct allegation against the RCMP. He referred to the Bronfman case a little while ago. In the Bronfman case, the Statistics Canada case, the Hamilton Harbour case, and in the dredging case, the hon. member has taken to himself credit for bringing these things to the public. The Commissioner of the RCMP has said, time and again, that the hon. member has not furthered these cases but that he has impeded them by bringing out six months' premature disclosures while the investigations were under way.
In the Bronfman case I replied to the hon. member as the parliamentary secretary in the way the hon. member indicated, but he came across the floor to me afterwards and showed me documents he had. They were indeed marked "Secret," but the documents stated something which was very ambiguous. They did not indicate that the RCMP was coercing Mr. Bronfman into not laying charges or into not going ahead. What really happened was that Mr. Bronfman took his case to the Federal Court of Canada. He decided to withdraw his case. He felt he did not have enough goods to go on, but this is the kind of allegation the hon. member for Central Nova continually makes. Hit and run, hit and run. He does not come across with any facts because he just does not have any.
The hon. member is not here now. Somebody said his office was bugged. I do not know what might be obtained from his office other than perhaps an allegation he might make against somebody, without any facts to back it up. He has never backed anything up in anything he has done.
One of the investigations the hon. member prompted with his questions in this House involved the Hamilton Harbour matter. The former solicitor general and the solicitor general at the time of this matter were questioned in the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. The hon. member ran out of questions, as did all the members of the opposition. As a matter of fact the solicitors general exonerated themselves completely and totally with respect to any allegations made at that time. They did so with respect to Statistics Canada, with respect to Mitchell Bronfman, and with respect to all the others. Hon. members opposite who make allegations should have the courage to present facts upon which those



October 31, 1977

allegations are based. It is great to come in with carloads of suspicion, but they come in with not even a wheelbarrow-full of truth, yet they build these things up far out of proportion.
The hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) spoke about the performance of the Solicitor General (Mr. Fox) today. I was elected in 1972, five years ago yesterday, and today was the first time 1 have seen a question period in this House in which all the questions from the great minds and intelligence of the opposition were directed to one minister alone. The unfair, unnecessary, and unwarranted attacks on the RCMP by hon. members opposite will take a long time for the RCMP to overcome. It is too bad that hon. members opposite do not realize the damage they are doing to one of the most respected police forces in the world. The president of Interpol is a former commissioner of the RCMP. Commissioner Higgitt's police force was recognized as the most efficient, honest, and honourable in the world. It is not we on this side who have been attacking this force and criticizing its operations. It has been members of the opposition, such as the hon. member for Central Nova and others who do not have the guts to come across with the facts they say they have. They really have no facts. They have only a hope and a desire to further their political careers by blackening and damaging one of the finest police forces in this world.
The hon. member for Central Nova has still not come forward with any facts with respect to Statistics Canada, the Mitchell Bronfman case, the dredging charges, or the Hamilton Harbour matter, but he throws irresponsible allegations around this House with careless abandon because he is not answerable.
This government has been answerable in this House for the actions of the RCMP. It is prepared to take it on the chin when the RCMP, through over-exuberance, moves across the line, as it has done in this case. Maybe it has committed an illegal act. 1 would rather have it that way than have the government in control of each and every operation of the police force in this country, or in the provinces of this country.
If we, as members of parliament, are going to insist that members of cabinet be in day-to-day charge of the operation of police forces, then I think we should take the criticism of those things they do wrong, and I think we should take accolades for those things they do right. If we begin to take charge of their operations this parliament will investigate a police state. I am not prepared to see that happen in this Canada that I love so well.
What is the alternative, Mr. Speaker? It is to have trust, faith and confidence in these officers who have made a career of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and of the municipal and provincial police forces of this country. The other alternative, according to the hon. member for Calgary North, the hon. member for Yukon, and the hon. member for Central Nova, would be to have the Solicitor General and other members of the cabinet direct the operations of this police force in criminal investigations, national security, customs and excise, and all such matters. This is not the role of parliament and it is not the role of a minister. A mandate must be given unequivocally, however, to the police department on what they should or should not do to carry out their functions within this country.
I believe that this parliament, especially in the field of criminal law, attempts to pass laws without reference to partisan political stances. I also believe that the police forces of this land should carry out their functions in the same way,

and I think they have done so. I think it is unfair for the opposition to harangue the RCMP continually, particularly because they cannot defend themselves. The Solicitor General in his speech today, and in answer to questions today, indicated that the actions taken in 1973 in the break-in at the Parti Quebecois offices was honestly believed, by those who did it, to be in the national interest. I think we will have to wait, and I am prepared to wait, for a legal process, a judge and jury, to determine whether there is guilt or innocence in the matter. I think it is time that members of the opposition began to conduct themselves with some forebearance, and gathered the facts before making reckless and careless accusations which are doing great harm to a great and highly respected police force in this country.

Mr. Speaker, I would say to the hon. member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Poulin) that my target is not the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. My target is this government which, through incompetence and worse than incompetence, has brought about the situation which precipitated this debate. The hon. member and others in the backbenches of the Liberal party share that responsibility with those in the frontbenches.
We have had some interesting comments in this debate. 1 listened to the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) with great wonderment as he laid down the criteria, and indisputably so, indicating what was political vetting of certain organizations in the past with respect to their capability to participate in public affairs and their probable danger to the state. Mr. Speaker, if that criteria had existed in 1963, '64 or '65, the man who went on to become the hon. member for Mount Royal and subsequently the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) of this country, would never have got into parliament.
I also heard the hon. member for Ottawa-Centre (Mr. Poulin) and the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. MacGuigan) labouring the question of Watergate. Obviously they are affected by Watergate and its similarity to the situation which exists here. The hon. member for Ottawa Centre said that the principles of Watergate do not apply to Canada because this government disclosed the facts. It only disclosed the facts and the Solicitor General (Mr. Fox) only disclosed his facts because he and members of the government knew that those facts were coming out in the inquiry in Montreal under Commissioner Keable. Knowing that, he cut his losses and made admissions about what is going on.
I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that as and when the commission in Montreal, and possibly the Laycraft commission in Edmonton, come to the point where they will be disclosing facts, such disclosures will be preceded by a statement in this House by the Solicitor General. It is only because
[Mr. Poulin.J
of that, and because of the fact that documents were made known, that public inquiries and/or prosecutions were undertaken in that long, sordid calendar of deception, corruption, and lying which surrounded the skirts of this government for the last five or six years.
The hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville laboured the point about this not being Watergate.
If the government wants to come clean, let it do so. The leader of this party (Mr. Clark), the hon. member for Gren-ville-Carleton (Mr. Baker), and other members of the party have requested a parliamentary committee. It is before a parliamentary committee that we should bring to judgment those ministers who might, under conditions and facts which are known, be tried for what I suggest are very serious political delinquencies. Let us establish a committee. Let it take from those ministers the powers of Crown privilege which they can exercise in debate and questioning. Let those members of government, from the Prime Minister down, be sworn and heard. Let the former commissioners, other officials attached, and the directors of the intelligence branch be brought before that committee. Let us find out how much was told, what information was given to members of government, from the Prime Minister down, at the pertinent times.
The government should set up such a committee with unrestricted terms of reference so that there is a fair and reasonable opportunity for questioning and challenging the truthfulness of statements made on the other side of this House. Only then can we say the government is coming clean by letting there be an investigation before a proper forum under terms of reference. This is essential if this issue is to be brought out in the open.
It was a pretty sad day for this House, after the Solicitor General had finished almost an hour of questions and answers this afternoon, when there was a spontaneous burst of applause from his colleagues. It was a considerable performance by the minister-subtle, brittle, evading the issues and not answering directly. Not one answer did the Solicitor General give today of facts not previously known. He did not, in one single answer, give us information we had sought. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that parliament was dragged to a very low level by that performance this afternoon. If this House is going to survive, question period must be more than entertainment. At the present time, because of the advent of television in the House, the tendency of the government and ministers to oscillate, to evade issues, to refuse to answer, to give incorrect answers to questions, is fortunately becoming more apparent to the public. The public of Canada is now having a chance to see what we have seen for many years, now-a government without the answers, without the capacity, and without the competence to do the job for which it was elected.
I say to the Solicitor General that it is not enough for him to do what he did this afternoon. There is a principle known to law, particularly to lawyers involved in insurance law, that it is not enough just not to tell lies; there must be no material
October 31, 1977

concealment; there must be full disclosure of the facts. This did not happen today. It rarely happens in this Chamber as far as ministers are concerned. That is a principle which I suggest ministers of the Crown should adopt so that the people might be able to feel greater confidence in those who govern their affairs.
I am a member of the opposition, but I say that the lack of confidence which exists all over the country in the government is a sad story. The government has addressed itself to various measures in an attempt to alleviate economic conditions. To my mind, the one element which is requisite if these measures are to take effect is confidence among the people in their government and in its proposals. Such confidence does not exist today and, until it does, we shall not make progress in overcoming the problems which face us.
Far from criticizing the RCMP, I pay tribute to them. I practised law for many years in a rural, frontier area, where it was not unknown for two-constable detachments to patrol thousands of square miles. They kept the faith, maintained the vigil, and had the support of the public. It was a great force, and I believe it still is. Basically, I believe it is still a sound force and one of the greatest in the world. Unfortunately, the treatment the government has meted out to it is such that, as my hon. friend from the Yukon said, it has lost its morale. There is anxiety.
I do not suggest the government has instigated some of the incidents to which we have been directing our attention, but I remember the play about Becket in which the King said, "Will no one rid me of this man?" And I suggest some of the things which were done by the RCMP or by this intelligence unit were performed in the expectation that they would be pleasing to the government.
Morale in the force will not be restored until the government makes some substantial changes. The fault really lies across the floor. The Prime Minister is alleged to have said in his press conference that police may break the law, sometimes. I challenge that assertion. There are no circumstances in which the police may break the law. The Solicitor General has suggested that if the law is not effective enough to give the police the weapons they need to combat organized crime, subversion, alleged terrorism, apprehended insurrection and so on, we should change the law. Well, if the government has facts upon which it can base this proposition that the law be changed, let us have those facts.
Others, beside myself, have spoken of the government's obsession with secrecy. Out of secrecy come corruption and incompetence-this government's record ever since it embraced secrecy as its watchword.
I shall not keep the House much longer. This has been a good debate. I suggest it will be useful and that it would probably obviate situations of the kind which have arisen so many times in the past if we had a reasonable law with regard to the freedom of information. I shall not pursue the issue, now, but there is no question in my mind but that the government has said "No" on three occasions. My sources tell me that before the last Speech from the Throne the govern-

ment said no, that it said no again just before the green paper was issued, and that it again said no just before the Speech from the Throne which we have recently finished discussing. Some of the younger cabinet ministers may have been in favour of it but the older members of the cabinet, those who have been there long enough to know what secrets are rattling around like skeletons in the closet, said no because they feared that a freedom of information law would make known things they do not wish to be made known to the public.
Other reasons have been advanced, of course. They have said that judges should not over-rule decisions of ministers. Mr. Speaker, I am told that in one department of the United States government, the Department of Justice, there are 55,000 people who have the right to put the stamp "Confidential" on a document, 18,000 with the right to put "Secret" on a document and 3,000 who have the right to mark documents "Top Secret". I do not know how many people have similar authority in this country, but I suggest that if civil servants are entitled to say a document should be marked confidential, an objective, independent judge should surely be entitled to say that, in his opinion, a certain document is one which should be made available to the public on request.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that we would not today be facing the situation which has developed if government, police forces, intelligence units, and senior civil servants knew that the things they did today might be made public tomorrow or the week afterward. Knowledge that what they did one day might be made public the next would encourage those concerned to make sure that their actions would bear the light of public scrutiny. Such a situation does not prevail at the present time.
In my view we cannot tolerate the continuation of the situation we have observed over the last months and years. It is for parliament, acting on behalf of the people of Canada, to lay down the rules and circumstances under which the police force must function. I realize that day-to-day implementation is a matter for the government, but it is a question of the conflict between various public interests. The widest possible public interest of the people of Canada lies in having a government and a police force which are subject to the laws of the land, and this must be maintained as against the narrower public interests of those who use the term "security" in order to engage in activities of the kind of which we have heard. I am afraid that all too often as far as the term "security" is concerned the government equates that word with the preservation of the Liberal party. It means something more than that.
Some method should be designed whereby this House, in the final analysis, has the right to maintain some watch over the public's money. We do not know how much money is spent or where it is spent. A committee of this House should be established under conditions which are susceptible to the security interests so that the public interest will be subject to the scrutiny and challenge by members of this House which it needs. If that is not done, this debate will have been fruitless.

We have had the strange spectacle of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) last Friday merely saying that these actions were "misguided". He left the very clear intimation in my mind that what was done was illegal. I am sure anyone who reads the press conference or who has heard the statement made by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Holt) this evening, which was echoed last night on

national television and again in this House today by the Solicitor General (Mr. Fox), will realize if what was done was illegal, then we really have only two alternatives because of the high motives of the people involved. Either we let the law enforcement agencies of this country continue to break the law themselves, in the belief that the national interest is a higher priority and more important than the mere imposition of those standards of legal observance that we have for everyone else, or the law should be changed. We have just heard an intimation of that as well from the previous speaker. In other words, there would be one standard of legal observance and lawful behaviour for those engaged in so-called national security, and a far higher one for ordinary citizens. As far as I am concerned, that is a double standard of behaviour.
The other alternative emanating from the Prime Minister and the Solicitor General is that perhaps the law should be changed to recognize this problem, and instead of merely tolerating the double standard I have indicated, we should recognize it and enshrine it in the law. According to the Prime Minister, these are the only two alternatives. Of course that is just simply not so.
There is another choice, and that is to make sure that the proven, experienced, just, and traditional criminal law of this land and country, and the common law which we follow, are enforced equally against everyone. There should be no exceptions, no interference, no double standards. In law enforcement, in my experienced opinion, there can be no fighting fire with fire. You do not rape to find a rapist. You do not use drugs to find those who are abusing our drug rules and laws. You do not blackmail to catch a blackmailer.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ILLEGAL ACTS COMMITTED BY FORCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
You can speak about terrorism, but you do not bomb to trap a bomber. Certainly you do not burgle to convict a burglar. It does not matter whether it is a major crime or a minor misdemeanour. It does not matter whether the allegation is the bugging of a member of parliament's office or whether it is a question of national security. The law is the law. It is open, known, fair, and impartial. The high and mighty, as well as the low and miserable, are equally bound. If they cannot fairly obey the law, then they cannot fairly enforce the law. This applies to the police, to security groups, and to governments.
Primarily what are we talking about in this debate? We are concerned about the incident in January of 1973 when a flagrantly lawless act occurred that cannot, on any grounds, be justified. What should have happened? The hon. member who preceded me poked fun at it in one way, and attempted to pour scorn on the legal procedures which should have been followed.
If the security officers had any sort of reasonable ground for believing that a crime had been committed, and that evidence of it could be found in a political party's office, then the security officers involved could have easily obtained from a justice of the peace a proper and legal search warrant. I do not care if it was a Parti Quebecois office, a Liberal office, a Conservative office, a Social Credit office or an NDP office.
October 31, 1977

I know a search warrant is just a scrap of paper in the eyes of some of the members. I know that the case in the eyes of some police officers, because I have had experience with them, is that it is merely a token, sometimes antiquated, certainly routine and, in many cases, a bothersome procedure. It is certainly a very irksome procedure to a police group in a hurry, and impatient to get a job done which they have been ordered to complete by their superiors. It may be irksome, but it is necessary because it is the law. The law in some instances may be an ass, but it is not up to a security group or the police to change it, or apply it to others and not themselves.
In this case the police did not follow the law. They broke in during the dead of night, which suggests in itself that they knew they were acting illegally. They put themselves above the law. To indicate that what they stole, copied, and then put back, was not a theft is simply ludicrous for anybody with any legal training and anybody with any responsibility, such as our Prime Minister has, especially in view of his training and in view of his past experience as the minister of justice.
The ameliorating thing in the eyes of some members opposite is the motive, that they were moved by a high ideal of national security. Motive simply does not enter into it. Whether it is dealing with national security or not, should any group be permitted to break the law which it has been sworn to enforce? There is little to suggest in this particular case that national unity was at stake. Should any group of security advisers-and that is what the security and intelligence service is-be permitted to go beyond the limits of the authority given to them, not by this government but by this parliament? This government is duty bound to enforce and to supervise, as trustees of this parliament and of our people as a whole, this security and intelligence service.
Can we afford the superciliousness and the callousness of the head of this government who indicated that if such a group breaks the law then they are not to blame, but somehow in this twisted and warped mental process he intimates that we are to blame because obviously the law should be changed? Obviously the people in charge should be changed, and not the law.
Since 1969 there have been serious problems that have not been resolved. I do not think there is a single member in the House who would stand up in his place tonight, no matter how forgiving he may be and no matter how much a lackey of the government he may be, who would indicate that since 1969 there have not been serious problems, or who would intimate that they were solved. There are serious problems that have not been resolved.
