warned all members of the House about the dangers of subversion. He tried to cloak the improprieties that have taken place by warning us not to rock the boat, not to give our enemies information which would be harmful to the state.
No member of parliament wants to attack the RCMP. Every member of parliament knows the role which the RCMP has played in this country. We respect the RCMP for the good things which it has done, but some of us expect the RCMP to obey the law, as we expect every citizen to preserve the law. If they break the law, in our opinion they must be criticized and they must be disciplined. That is why we are having this debate tonight and that is what the government obviously does not want to discuss.
While the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) was speaking, the Solicitor General interjected several times. He challenged the description of the APLQ or the PQ break-in and challenged the suggestion that these were in fact break-ins. I am not a lawyer, but if it was not breaking and entering, I would like to know what it was.
Let me quote from an article in the Globe and Mail of Saturday, October 29. One of the main stories there is headed, "RCMP Broke Into PQ Office Without Warrant, Fox Says". The article begins:
The Royal Canadian Mounted Police entered a Montreal office of the Parti Quebecois without a warrant on January 9, 1973, and removed, copied, and returned PQ membership lists, Solicitor General Francis Fox said yesterday.
If that is not breaking and entering, I wonder what it is. Later the same story reads:
Asked if he felt an illegal act had been committed, Mr. Fox replied that a judge must decide.
Surely nobody in this country has the right to break into premises. Surely people are entitled to the protection of the law from anybody who takes upon themselves the right to break into their premises. Does the Solicitor General believe that any police, including the RCMP, should have the power to enter the premises of organizations or individuals, to take documents or records, whenever they believe it is necessary or useful, without authorization from the appropriate ministers of the Crown, without the authorization of judges?
If the RCMP believe that the Parti Quebecois was somehow subversive, why did they not apply for a search warrant? The Solicitor General and the Prime Minister have talked about the climate of the times. This break-in did not occur in 1970. It did not occur at the time of the kidnappings in October of 1970. We were not faced, as the minister at that time, who has now gone to his reward in the Senate, said, with thousands, literally thousands of revolutionaries who were going to destroy this country. We are talking about 1973, and we are talking about a party which every member of this parliament, regardless of party, disagrees with, a party which believes in the separation of the province of Quebec from Canada. But surely that is their right. Surely in a democratic system they have the right to advocate separation of their province. The Prime Minister said as much on Saturday.

October 31, 1977


He said that he told the RCMP to cease and desist when he found out they were doing it. The hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Holt), the one-term member, contradicted the Prime Minister when she suggested that she did not mind if the RCMP were to keep tabs on the Parti Quebecois. Of course she does not mind, that is typical Liberalism. If you disagree with Liberals, you are a subversive.
Is the Parti Quebecois subversive? If it is not, why did the RCMP feel that it had the right to steal the membership list of the PQ? Is it illegal for people in Quebec or anywhere else to make contributions of money to the PQ? If not, why did the RCMP feel that they had the right to steal the lists of contributors of money to the PQ?
My colleague, the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt), revealed tonight that labour leaders in B.C. were being investigated by the RCMP. Labour leaders in B.C. and in other provinces disagree with the government's anti-inflation program. Is that illegal? Is that subversive?
The hon. member for the Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) referred to the investigation by the security forces of the Indian Association of Alberta. Is it illegal or subversive for the Indian Association of Alberta to feel that the Indians in this country have been mistreated? I find it hard to understand why one arm of the government, the security forces, would be investigating the Indian Association of Alberta, while another arm of the government, the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, appoints the president of the Indian Association of Alberta to be their director of its department in charge of the spending of all the money that goes from the federal government to the native people of Alberta, to make him the director of the department for the whole province of Alberta.
The government does not know the difference between dissent which is permissible in a democratic society, and subversion. It is not surprising. Members of the Liberal party have formed the government of this country for 50 of the last 60 years and they think that anybody who disagrees with them is subversive. Some of us believe that democracy means that people who disagree with us have a right to express their views and to believe that the police will not interfere with their rights.
The Solicitor General and other members of the Liberal party who have spoken tonight have tried to create the impression that, as soon as the government found out about the improprieties, the break-ins, the arson, the burning and the stealing of dynamite in which the RCMP was apparently involved, they came to parliament and they told the people of Canada all about it and that they disapproved of it and would stop it. The facts are entirely different. The government did not voluntarily tell the people of Canada that the representatives of the three police forces, the RCMP, the Quebec Provincial Police and the Montreal Police, had broken into the APLQ offices. No, that information came out when an RCMP officer, who was involved in a bombing which had nothing to do with politics, bungled the job, wound up in hospital and, when arrested and tried for the bombing, blurted out that he and other officers had been involved in that break-in. That is

when the government decided it had to tell the people of Canada, not until then.
When the representatives of the three police forces were charged and brought to court, and when they pleaded guilty, what did the government say about that? Did the government say to the officer concerned, "You should not have done that, you broke the law, you were involved in an illegal act. We are going to discipline you"? Oh, no, it did not do that at all. It let him keep the promotion which he had received. What did the people of Canada believe? What can they believe? They can only believe that the government approved of what he did. Otherwise hoe could it have permitted him to get a promotion and keep it?
We are told now that the government is giving the public information about RCMP involvement in burning a barn and in the theft of dynamite. I wish that, instead of the nonsense that we heard from the parliamentary secretary, he had addressed himself to the actual cases and he had the guts to defend those actions of the RCMP if he really believed that they were proper or necessary. However, he did not do that. He talked in vague generalities because he did not have the courage to say what he really believed; either that, or he did not know what he was talking about.
Did the government come forward voluntarily to tell the people of Canada about these illegal acts committed by RCMP officers? No, it did not do that. Why are we getting the information now? Because the government knows that the commission appointed by the government of Quebec has the power of subpoena, it has access to the files of the ministry of justice of Quebec and has access to the files of the Quebec Provincial Police. The government knows that many of the illegal actions in which police were involved will undoubtedly become public, as will some of the illegal actions of the police in the province of Alberta which will come out during the Laycraft Inquiry, despite everything the Solicitor General is doing to try to choke that inquiry off.
It is because this information is going to become public that the government has moved to tell the people of Canada about illegal acts. I do not know whether the government ordered them, but its silence until now makes it clear to anybody who wants to look at the records that the government at least condoned those illegal acts.
The minister regretted the fact that opposition members, according to him, were not being constructive. Of course any time one criticizes a Liberal government, the least he is accused of is that he is not being constructive. The most the government will accuse a person of, if it can, is that he is being subversive.
I think that there are several fundamental principles we can recommend to the Solicitor General, if he really wants advice, and it seems to me that they are very simple. First, all Canadians must observe and obey the laws of Canada. I ask the Solicitor General to consider this question sometimes. How can he expect the people of Canada to observe the law and live

October 31, 1977

by the law if the police, who have the responsibility of enforcing the law, are permitted to break the law, as some police officers have done? If the police who break the law are not disciplined and, indeed, rewarded, what happens to the rule of law?
It is not good enough for the Solicitor General to say he will wait for the royal commission to make its findings. The royal commission has the job of finding out how many times this happened, how it happened and why it happened, but the Solicitor General does not have to wait until the royal commission makes its report before he disciplines people in the police force who have broken the law.
If the security services find that the present laws do not give them the power or authority to do their job-this was a suggestion made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), to protect the citizens because he thinks the law as it is now written restricts the activities of these security services too closely-surely the proper procedure is not to say that the police have to break the law. Surely this government, which may know or may think that the police do not have the authority they need, should have come to parliament, told parliament that the police do not have the authority they need, and proposed changes in the laws. That is the way a democratic government should operate. Did we get that kind of action from the government? Of course not. When the illegal acts of the police become known we get this stupid belated rewriting of the facts we have had here tonight and in the last few days.
The second concrete suggestion I make to the government is that it rethink its concept of democracy. It should realize that even though the Liberal party has been in power for 50 of the last 60 years, we still live in a democratic society. People have a right to disagree with governments, even Liberal governments.
People have a right to express their views and to publicize their position and to do this freely, without secret investigation by the police and security forces of this country. If the Solicitor General and the government would keep those two basic principles in mind and live by them, we would not have the distasteful task we have had the last few days, and the one we are doing tonight, of criticizing a few members of a police force which has had a wonderful record in this country.
The police have a job to do. Their job is one which the government should outline for them. The basic principles they should follow should be made clear by the government. We have had enough cover-ups by the government and acts which ought not to have taken place. I hope-although I did not get much of the impression that the government really understands how things have gone wrong-that the government will take the time to rethink what has happened, to re-evaluate what has happened and to take steps to change the law, if that is necessary, and to see that the laws of this country and their administration are handled in a way which will bring pride to people in a democratic society rather than the way we have seen revealed in the last few days.

Just listen to me. 1 have only 18 minutes left. You will hear a few charges.
I just finished reading a book about the Nixon years in the United States entitled "The Time of Illusion", by Jonathan Schell. 1 recommend hon. members to get this book because much of the paranoia in evidence in the United States during those years, which is analyzed in this book, is present now in

October 31, 1977

Canada with this government, and hon. gentlemen opposite should start getting wise to themselves.
My position on the whole business of the RCMP and illegal break-ins can be summed up with a quotation from pages 379 and 380 near the end of this book. The author says:
On the other hand, it is not the purpose of these remarks to in any way excuse the political actors of the period-some of whom were also key strategists-from responsibility on the ground that they did what they did in the cause of human survival.
There is a lot of similarity between what this government is saying and the situation described here. This government wants to intimate that it is the question of human survival that causes it to do these things in the name of security.
He continues:
All governments have their burdens to bear and their decisions to make, and if the heaviness of the responsibilities were to be considered justification for repressive action, no country would remain free. A free country does not place responsibilities in one of the scales and the liberties of the people in the other. It holds to the faith that only in an atmosphere of freedom can the responsibilities be squarely met.
It applies directly to this situation when he says:
A free country does not place responsibilities in one of the scales and the liberties of the people in the other.
That is what the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is doing. That is what the Solicitor General is doing in the argument he presented to the House. He says this is in the cause of national security.
At this press conference the Prime Minister showed his disdain for the intelligence of the Canadian people and for this House. He shows nothing but ennui, and disdain for members of the House and the people of Canada. When it came out at the press conference that the RCMP security branch had illegally entered premises and taken the membership lists of a democratically formed political party in Quebec, copied them and put them back again-well, Mr. Speaker, that is break and entry. It is theft.
Then we found out they burned down a barn. That is arson. What did the Prime Minister say about that? He started talking about a city. What would you do if somebody was smuggling an atom bomb and you discovered it? Would you break into his place before he set it off? That is the Prime Minister's example. We are supposed to equate that with the RCMP breaking into the offices of the Parti Quebecois and taking the membership lists. What are we supposed to be? What are members of cabinet and of the Liberal caucus supposed to be if they are to listen to that kind of nonsense from the Prime Minister? He is so contemptuous of us that he thinks he can get away with anything.
I have a transcript of the press conference here, but the Prime Minister is not present to defend his actions or the actions of his ministers. He does not want to meet us face to face and argue with us; he just argues with the press. There he has the upper hand because he can say the press conference is over. On page four of the transcript he says:
[Mr. Crosbie.J
I think if in circumstances like that the law has to be broken technically in order to save a city, then I think either it should be broken technically or the law should be changed ...
I am sure I agree that if somebody had an atom bomb and is about to set it off, I would approve the RCMP rushing in illegally to stop him, and so would everybody else. But, Mr. Speaker, that has nothing to do with breaking into the premises of a political party and the kind of activity that has apparently been going on.
There are three issues here. First is the dissembling of the government, its lack of concern about the administration of justice. The ministers who are responsible for the administration of justice have nothing but contempt for it. As I watched the Solicitor General today I thought the fetish of the fox must be the stonewall. He was not at all concerned about the reputation of the RCMP, the reputation of security agencies, or the reputation of the government. That is shocking, Mr. Speaker.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford), who is sworn to uphold the law, is not in his place, and the Prime Minister, the big culprit, is out talking with Premier Lougheed when he should be in this House giving us an explanation. This shows a lack of concern about the administration of justice and a lack of care about the RCMP. Then they have the gall to accuse the opposition of attacking the RCMP. They show a lack of care about parliamentary government and democratic liberties. The Prime Minister was the author of articles in Cite Libre-now it is Cuba Libre. Where is he when we are talking about our democratic liberties in this House?
The second issue, Mr. Speaker, is the effect of being too long in power. This is government by disdain. The Prime Minister's statement reeks of disdain-"You are going to put up with me, Emperor Trudeau, no matter what I say or do." This shows arrogance and cynicism. On television you can see the cynical boredom of it all-the boredom of having to answer these questions, having to deal with these fools of reporters, these incompetent fools in the opposition. He does not mind the fools in his own caucus because he finds them even easier to deal with. He is like the Roman emperor who made his horse a Senator. He does not care who he has in the cabinet, how wooden headed they are, how incompetent, how lazy, how stupid-he does not care about that.
The third issue is the cover-up. This is Trudeaugate, not Watergate. It is a cover-up in this House in interfering with royal commissions. Is nobody shocked when they pick up the newspaper and read a heading "Ottawa Blocks Alberta Probe Into RCMP, Tax Activities" in the Globe and Maill It refers to the solicitors general and a former minister of revenue firing off affidavits to stop a provincial royal commission from finding out whether the RCMP was involved with certain Winnipeg policemen and what happened in a secret agreement between the RCMP and the Department of National Revenue.
The article alleges that a civil servant admittedly lied. One Edmund Swatzack, a federal tax investigator, lied about the fact that wiretaps were given to the Department of National Revenue when he was first questioned about them. An RCMP
October 31, 1977

inspector, Graham George, overseer of the probe admitted under questioning:
... When the RCMP knows they can't wiretap under the tax act, they look for a Criminal Code violation and then the information gathered is used for income tax ...
This is in Canada where the government is supposed to be responsible to parliament. Our system has gone completely off the rails. We do not have the checks and balances of the United States constitution. We do not have congressional committees-in this House we have eunuchs, not committees. They have no power and can do nothing when there is a majority government.
Not one government backbencher got up tonight and showed concern or alarm about this. Not even one who is a former law dean expressed any disquiet about it.
What is happening about this RCMP inspector and this federal tax investigator who has admitted lying? How is it that a Corporal Williams of the RCMP made a statement in March that on one occasion he had searched rooms under instructions from another constable and then, when testifying before an inquiry in June, he could no longer remember whether he had made a sweep? Is the royal commission to be allowed to get to the bottom of this, or is the stonewalling going to extend to that as well? What can anyone reading this newspaper think of our system of justice, Mr. Speaker? Why should we assume that anyone is going to observe the law if he can get away with not observing it?
These things are scandalous. Twenty years ago each incident would have made the headlines, but today nobody seems to care. The one who cares least is the Solicitor General who had the gall to stonewall all day and give these false arguments tonight, but no information.
The Prime Minister does not care. He only has disdain for the House and for us. What are they doing about John C. Doyle, one of the contributors to the Liberal party, who owes $3.5 million in income tax for 20 years and still does not pay. One case was heard last week when the judges threw out a spurious appeal, but there is another case to go. For 20 years income tax and interest have not been collected from John C. Doyle, a fugitive from justice whom the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) in his latest book shows was heavily involved in certain peculiar events surrounding this House in 1963 and 1965. That is the kind of justice we have in Canada.
If you are on medium income or are poor, they put the old justice right to you, but if you are in the security forces, or if you are John C. Doyle, you are treated with kid gloves. If the people of Canada do not want to correct that, I suppose we can only shrug our shoulders and say we all have to get along.
The next thing is, they will be bugging us. They have already bugged the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay). Lo and behold, they are bugging poor old Central Nova.

I say they are bugging. I cannot say it is the government bugging him. I don't know who else is being bugged. I am afraid I haven't been bugged, but I hope they find a bug when I ask them to look for one.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in the Globe and Mail of October 29 we read: "Fox Reveals Break-in." The fearful Fox, or fretful Fox, only revealed that break-in when he knew it would be revealed in any event. Asked if the mounties had broken into the headquarters of other political parties, such as the New Democratic Party, Mr. Fox said, and I quote: "We have made inquiries about headquarters of other parties and the answer is no. That is, to the best of our knowledge."
He is pretty careful. He cannot even guarantee that the RCMP had not broken into the headquarters of the New Democratic Party much less the Progressive Conservative headquarters, or the United News in Agony from Unemployment Headquarters, or whatever headquarters they are going to break into next. No the Solicitor General cannot guarantee that the RCMP have not broken into the New Democratic Party headquarters. That is what that statement in quotation marks tells me. "Not to the best of our knowledge". He should have said, "No, they've never broken into the New Democratic Party headquarters, and they never will break into the headquarters of the New Democratic Party as long as I am Solicitor General. I will protect the right of the New Democratic Party members to be wrong." But he did not say that.
Mr. Speaker, is it not peculiar that these events all happened in the province of Quebec? Is it because the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is just mesmerized by the province of Quebec? Anything goes in Quebec. It is like a foreign country. In the United States they can do anything outside the U.S., but they are not supposed to operate in the U.S. In Canada they can do anything they like in Quebec because the Prime Minister is obsessed with the Parti Quebecois. He is afraid he cannot meet them on their own terms. He says they can separate and there won't be violence used to stop them. He says there won't be force if they can persuade a majority to support them. The Prime Minister has conceded that, but then he turns around and apparently permits every kind of action to be taken to thwart them behind the scenes. It is because he is absolutely mesmerized by Quebec that all he can see is the problem in Quebec. He is afraid he cannot deal with it in a normal democratic way or on the hustings. That is why the Prime Minister is using all these other tactics. All those incidents we know most about-the arson, the break and enter, the theft, have all taken place in Quebec. There was one in Toronto, but most of them have occurred in Quebec because of this preoccupation of the Prime Minister.
I do not care what happens. If this House and if the government and the people agree that the Parti Quebecois are free to organize in the proper manner and to use reason-not to use force-to try to persuade their people to separate, then illegal means should not be used to try to prevent this. The Solicitor General himself in his speech last Friday was discussing what the security force can do. I refer to page four of his speech. He said that they can ascertain and assess the nature



of the separatist threat in Canada with a view to identifying individual groups and organizations whose real or apparent purpose was to subvert or destroy by force, by violence or by threats of force or violence, Canada as a united country. No one has brought forward any evidence that the Parti Quebecois has, as an objective or purpose, the destruction of Canada as a united country by force or by violence or by threats of force or violence. That is just not the case.
There is no excuse. These are directives given to the RCMP. They are the same as those given on March 27, 1975 for the same purpose when describing what the security service can do. It had to be clear to the security branch and the RCMP that they cannot and there is no justification for them breaking the law in connection with the Parti Quebecois.
At least President Nixon taped himself, not just the opposition. One can only hope that there will be a few tapes in the future from which we might be able to get the truth, tapes of the Solicitor General and the Prime Minister not just tapes of the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) and a few others.
As far as the RCMP is concerned, everyone has been careful to say that they are not attacking the RCMP. Well, nor am 1, Mr. Speaker. The RCMP is a fine police force, but I look at all police forces with a healthy scepticism and I am not afraid to say it. 1 have no fetish about the RCMP, and if members of the RCMP are going about Canada committing illegal acts in the manner we have evidence they have done in three or four instances, then 1 say the RCMP have to be brought to heel. They have to be brought to heel, and their political masters who encouraged them, or who are hiding them, or who directed them or who condoned those acts, have to be brought to heel also.
I believe this has been a valuable debate but it will be all to no purpose unless it helps change the government at the next election or unless some of the members opposite, when they go to caucus, do something to bring this lot to heel. If they are not prepared to do it here in the House then it must be done in caucus. Something has got to be done to shake them up. They are the only ones who can do it since everyone here knows that the government can do what it likes so long as it has a majority here. It is only some of its own members in caucus who can put a stop to it.
I suppose some may think that what we are doing here is a waste of time, Mr. Speaker. We are just putting our case on the record. But I am sure that there must be many members on the government side who must be just as dissatisfied with the kind of leadership they are getting and the kind of incidents that are going on. It has not yet reached the point reached in the Nixon affair, but that started out by people breaking the law in small ways, realizing that they had enemies and looking into tax files and all the rest. Look where it finally got them, Mr. Speaker. The same thing can happen with this government. The more it gets away with the worse it will get.
It is time the government came to its senses and gave us the whole story. Otherwise it is time for Liberal members to do

something about it in caucus or for the people of Canada to terminate the regime of the members opposite. It is tired, disdainful, arrogant, worn out, and uncaring.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the debate which has been going on all evening has now lasted well into the morning hours, it now being about 11 minutes to two. However, I think it has been a very worth-while debate and I hope that the members of the press will draw to the attention of the people of this country the seriousness of what we are discussing tonight.
For a number of years I was a schoolteacher. For several years in the riding 1 represent the incidence of breaking and entering on the part of teenagers has been on the increase. A lot of people in the community are becoming very concerned about this serious criminal activity. Yet the matter we are now considering involves, among other things, the conviction of three members of the RCMP, I believe, on charges of breaking and entering. In this case, though, for some reason or other, they were given a discharge or a conditional discharge-I do not know what the exact term is. Even though they were convicted, they were exonerated under the law. How do we address ourselves to the young people of this country when, on one hand, three law enforcement officers, presumably instructed by officials senior to them to break the law, are exonerated, when a 14 or 17 year old who breaks and enters a public or private residence is given two days, two weeks, two months, or whatever the sentence may be?
I am starting out on a very personal note this evening because I think we have to talk in terms of people. We have to talk in terms of how the law is applied to individuals. It is not so much how we philosophize on general principles and how those laws are applied to the people as a whole.
When I go home tomorrow, I may find a young man or young woman coming into my office and saying, "Why were those three RCMP officers given virtually carte blanche to break the law? When I stole a bicycle on November 12, 1975, I got a criminal record. I had to pay a fine or go to jail for a certain length of time." I will find that very difficult.
What we are talking about tonight goes beyond the individual, although I have the utmost respect for, and indeed our democratic system in this country must depend on, individual freedom and liberty. What we are talking about is essentially a conflict between how we define a security system under the law and how we protect people from that system.
I am quite convinced, although some of my colleagues might not agree with me on this point, that unfortunately we are living in an age where violence, terrorism, hijacking, spiriting people away and hiding them for 60, 80 or 90 days, and kidnapping, are commonplace. We do not know exactly how to cope with the situation.
October 31, 1977

I submit that we need to have a security system in a democracy, but where does the responsibility lie in this kind of arrangement? 1 charge the government with not really knowing where the responsibility lies. We have the RCMP and certain other security organizations within the government and the office of the Solicitor General (Mr. Fox). However, members on both sides of this House, and I presume 1 speak on behalf of the people of Canada, do not know where the responsibility lies.
You can talk about MI-5, the Security Intelligence Service, the Deuxieme Bureau, all the security agencies in England, France, Italy, Germany and so on. We also have to address ourselves to the reality that we live in a world where there is espionage, terrorism, and covert activity. This country so far has been reasonably blessed with very few outbreaks of terrorism, hijackings, skyjackings and so on.
Where do we, as legislators in a democracy, draw the line? It is my opinion that the government by default tries to pass the blame whenever something happens such as the PQ office break-in in Montreal. Whenever the RCMP security and intelligence branch breaks into an office and somebody feeds the information to the press or a member of parliament, the government backtracks and says it is not its responsibility. Ministers say they knew nothing about it until it came to their attention last night, or somebody telephoned at eleven o'clock that morning.
The government puts the blame on the security system within the RCMP. However, if, and I say this hypothetically, some subversive element in this country were to be caught in the act, I am quite sure that those people opposite who are condemning the RCMP would take the credit for stopping that illegal activity. This puts the RCMP in a very embarrassing position.
I think we have the best police forces in the world at all levels of law enforcement in this country. Some may disagree. When talking about the township, county, regional, provincial or federal level, you find that in spite of our criminal justices system, which is lacking terribly in the due process, we have outstanding members in our police forces. That is why I find it difficult to condemn the RCMP out of hand. That is not what I am doing. That is why I stood up earlier on a point of order. I was not criticizing the RCMP per se. I was simply pointing out that three officers had in fact admitted to a criminal offence and had been convicted of that offence.
It is not easy today in our society to maintain law and order. We are the civil authority in this country as far as the Criminal Code is concerned. That goes for both sides of this House. I often have the impression that for some reason or other members opposite, specifically those on the Treasury Benches, members of the cabinet, have the idea that they are the only lawmakers in this country.
We are the lawmakers of this country. We have the right to stand up and speak our mind. That is exactly what I am doing tonight. However, how far does it go? For example, I see the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) sitting opposite at this late hour. As a cabinet minister, I congratulate him for

being here at this late hour, and I say that in all honesty and integrity. But not too long ago the minister was minister of "unemployment", I think it was in those days, and of manpower, and we did have a problem.

speechtext: Don't tell me we are going to hear all about Tran Van Quang.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ILLEGAL ACTS COMMITTED BY FORCE
speechtext:
Yes, we are going to hear about Dang Van Quang again. 1 understand he has changed his name, is alive and well, and living somewhere in Montreal.
I will deal briefly with this because it relates to the RCM Police. At that time the minister was responsible, not for the RCM Police but for the Department of Manpower and Immigration. As a member of the House of Commons I could get no official information about what the RCM Police had done with respect to this former South Vietnamese general who was obviously implicated in the narcotics industry of Southeast Asia.
I am not blaming the minister specifically for this. 1 do not know whether he himself could find out; I have an idea he could not. I have an idea that the RCM Police did not have that information. If they had, they may not have given it to him anyway. This leads me to the argument I am making now, that the RCM Police will give certain ministers of the Crown certain information that the RCM Police think they should have.
I ask, Mr. Speaker, who runs the country? Is it those of us who are democratically elected, or those of us who are members on the government side, or more specifically those of us who are members of cabinet? We on this side, and I dare say the press, do not know whether or not cabinet ministers can dial a certain number at the RCM Police and say, "I want the facts and I want them fast. I want all the facts".

That would not be allowed, and a minister would not even try to do that, in the U.K. parliament, but it was tried here so that the statement could get on the floor on a Friday afternoon. That was done so that when the Thibault Commission meets this week there will at least be a semblance of disclosure.
The Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General (Mr. Blaker) tried to say that it has been an accusation of the opposition that wrongdoing was committed by members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Well, I was down in Room 130-S on Friday and heard the Solicitor General himself condemn the RCMP when asked whether the acts were illegal. When asked whether those actions had been legalized by the issue of a warrant he said, "Well, I wouldn't be here if that were the case". In other words, there would have been no reason for the Solicitor General to come before parliament unless he was prepared-as he was here on Friday and as he did downstairs before national television-to make the first accusations against the RCMP. The parliamentary secretary is shaking his head. He is entitled to do that. I think he should take a look at the transcript. I was there, and I saw that story being made.
Given that situation, the other matter with respect to the Parliament of Canada is the parliamentary secretary saying in this place, which we call the highest court in the country when it is convenient, that somehow it is improper or wrong for a member of parliament from any side of this House to stand up and ask a question about the activities of any Canadian employed in the Public Service of Canada.

The parliamentary secretary came awfully close to it. He talked about the damage to reputation either through debate or through questions in this House. He just finished doing that, and surely he cannot hold to that view. If he does-and I do not believe he does; I think in that sense he was defending the indefensible-then surely he is wrong and he must admit that.
The parliamentary secretary is right that the word "cover-up" has been used in the course of this debate. Cover-up is a word which has acquired its own particular meaning because of certain things which occurred in the southern part of North
(Mr. Baker (Grenville-Carleton).]
America to which this matter has been likened, rightly or wrongly, and 1 am not impressed with the pedantic arguments about whether it should be compared with Watergate. It really does not matter with what label it is painted; the fact is that a question has been raised in this House about the breadth of the terms of reference and whether they should be broadened to drive out of the mind of the most suspicious-not just in this House but outside as well-the thought that perhaps the terms of reference of the McDonald Commission are so narrow that they could reasonably be construed by the commissioners to apply only to the activities of the RCMP.
Incidentally, I say to the parliamentary secretary that that in itself could be an implied accusation by the government against the RCMP. I do not think it is fair that in the circumstances of this case there should be any doubt or even a difference of opinion between the government and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) on the breadth of the terms of reference. I think the government should move immediately to broaden them. In his speech today the Leader of the Opposition indicated how far he thought they should be broadened. If we are to err in this House in terms of that investigation, we ought to err in giving the broadest possible powers. That is not an unreasonable request, and when there is this question, when there is this doubt, and when there are reputations at stake I cannot understand why there is not the broadest possible opportunity to look into the question of ministerial responsibility.
What passed between the ministers and the security service and the security service and the RCMP? If anything passed, what was it? Surely the ministers have a responsibility.
The interesting thing about all this is that the two former ministers who could perhaps cast the best light on what went on in this debate did not step forward. Those two ministers have been sitting together as seat mates and, I suppose, soul mates. They sat listening to the debate but did not leap to their feet saying, "This is my position-this is what I knew, not about l'Agence de Presse Libre, about which statements were made on former occasions, but about the things said in this debate tonight." But they said nothing, Mr. Speaker. What is anybody to think about such silence? That is where the cover-up comes in, because the government has not come clean.
The minister didn't come completely clean in his statement to the House today, even though he was on his feet for an hour and subjected to questions. If he had the issue would not still be in the news at eleven o'clock tonight. There it stands, and the government has the answer. As long as that is unanswered an accusation is implied-and perhaps more strongly than that-against the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
One of the problems with this government is that while things are going well ministers take the credit, but when things start to go to hell they suddenly become innocent bystanders. I think we have to consider the position of the government then.
October 31, 1977

The hon. member for Niagara Falls (Mr. Young) asked in a humorous fashion whether the Solicitor General (Mr. Fox) should have knowledge of any matter undertaken by any agent or agency under his control. He expected me to answer yes to that question, but we know that is physically impossible. The minister cannot have such knowledge but, Mr. Speaker, he must have responsibility, and that is the issue in this case.
It has always been the tradition in our parliamentary system and in all parliaments in the Commonwealth, that a minister has responsibility for what happens in his department, even though he may not have knowledge. That applies here. Of course the minister cannot have knowledge, but he has ultimate responsibility. Of all the things in which the government is involved, it is inevitable that security activities will be primarily the responsibility of the executive branch and that, no matter what devices we think of, parliament can never have any great control over those security services. These things are given to a government willingly, on trust, but when that trust is violated, when a bug is found in a member's office-whether a government agency put it there God only knows-but when there are questions of agencies of government being involved in illegal acts, then that trust must be said to be violated. The government then owes this House and the people of Canada an explanation.
Thus far in this debate and during the question period today we have not been given an explanation. I say to them and to the parliamentary secretary who did his best to defend the indefensible, that the government's perspective in this matter is not in keeping with what I like to think are the traditions and demands of a democratic society.
What has happened, unfortunately, is that this defensive government, this secretive government, this arrogant government has somehow equated its interest with the national interest, and that is wrong, Mr. Speaker. That is the dilemma the government faces, not the dilemma put by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General. The government violated the most sacred trust given to it by a trusting people- to keep control of the security services of the country. There is

no other way they can be controlled, Mr. Speaker. The government violated that trust, and I say with respect to the Solicitor General, his predecessors and any ministers involved, even to the highest minister, that being the case, they are not fit for office. They are nice men and good to their families I suppose, but they are not fit for office. That is the issue we have to address.
The parliamentary secretary spoke of the need for security balanced against individual rights. I regard it as one of my individual rights that the security service will never overstep itself. I am not satisfied that this will not happen. I am not satisfied with the defence put up by the government.
The issue is simply ministerial responsibility. Either ministers knew and are part of the cover-up, or did not know and are incapable of supervising the most sensitive part of their departmental operations. In either event the ministry is wrong and the ministry should be ashamed of itself. It has let itself down, it has let this parliament down, and it has let the people of this country down. It will be answerable to those people for what has occurred.
I do not blame the RCMP, but they, like everybody else, are subject to the rule of law. The ministers have the ultimate responsibility for what must be done in this regard, however, and they will have to bear the ultimate burden for their failure to exercise it.
Before I go, Mr. Speaker, on behalf of all members of the House I should like to express to you and to the staff who have served us well and long this evening and morning, our grateful thanks.

Pursuant to Standing Order 26(13) I am satisfied that the debate has been concluded. I therefore declare the motion carried.
The House stands adjourned until two o'clock this afternoon.
